title: Throughput vs Cost: Prefetch & KV Demo with Orion Health
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Orion Health through a targeted Optimize demo focusing on prefetch/prefix strategies and KV cache sizing. Main concerns were latency SLAs for clinical workflows, cost per 1M tokens, and VPC deployment constraints. Action items: provide tailored cost simulation, share security pack, and schedule pilot benchmark next week.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — we got Priya, Samir, Dana, Jon from Orion, and Liam and I from Redwood. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Priya (Orion): Hi, thanks. Doing well. Excited to see the prefetch demo — we've been trying to balance our clinician latency target of <200ms with cost.
[00:22] Liam (Redwood SE): Awesome, that's exactly what we planned to focus on — tradeoffs between prefetch/prefix cache and KV cache sizing, plus some cost sims in the console. I will share my screen in a sec.
[00:31] Samir (Orion): Quick note — we run in a VPC with a private control plane, and we have strict data residency in our east-us-2 region. Any routing changes need to respect that.
[00:42] Maya: Totally noted, Samir. We'll show the Private deployment options and how the prefetching suggestions are region-aware.
[00:48] Liam: (screen shares) Okay, opening the Optimize tab — this is a demo account with a small model fleet. First slide, the high level: prefetching meaning creating warm KV snapshots for frequent prefixes, prefix cache is a read cache for repeated conversation starts, and KV cache is the per-session keyvalue kv state.
[01:10] Jon (Orion): Wait you said KV as "kay-vee" right? Sometimes our notes say K V cash — transcription is weird.
[01:16] Liam: (laughs) Yes, KV cache, not cash. Apologies for the ASR.
[01:20] [01:20] Liam: The basic idea: if you can identify common initial prompts or system messages — like triage templates clinicians use — you can precompute KV snapshots and reduce forward pass tokens and latency.
[01:33] Priya: For our triage flow, average prompt length is about 120 tokens, and expected final generation is another 80 tokens. Our p95 latency target is 180ms when routing to a 4096 model.
[01:45] Liam: Ok — quick back of envelope: with prefix prefetching you can cut 30–50% of tokens per request on those flows, and that translates directly to per-token cost decreases and latency reduction because the model does fewer autoregressive steps.
[01:58] [01:58] Maya: We'll jump into the console cost sim in a moment. Before that, a quick qualification question — how bursty is traffic? Do you have steady clinic hours or massive spikes?
[02:08] Samir: Mostly 8a–6p weekdays with peaks at 9am and 3pm. Spikes are about 4–5x baseline.
[02:14] Liam: Good to know. That affects batching window choices. Shorter windows help latency but reduce batching efficiency.
[02:22] [02:22] (crosstalk) Dana (Security): quick security flag — we need to ensure prefetch snapshots are not persisted outside KMS-managed storage. Are snapshots encrypted with customer keys?
[02:32] Harper (Redwood Product): Yes, optional KMS integration is supported for Private deployments; snapshots and cache artifacts can be encrypted with your customer-managed keys. We'll attach the security slide after the call.
[02:44] [02:44] Liam: Switching to the cost model — console shows baseline numbers for our curated model, then we overlay prefetch savings. I'm going to pick a sample workload: 10k requests/day, 120/80 tokens per request, and we'll simulate three strategies: (A) no prefetch, (B) prefix prefetch of top 10 templates, (C) prefix prefetch + 2MB KV warmers per session.
[03:10] Priya: Can you explain what you mean by 2MB KV warmers per session? That seems large.
[03:16] Liam: Sure, sorry poor phrasing — that's 2 MB of KV state total across shards for long sessions (i.e., many user turns). For your triage flows typical sessions are small, but for longitudinal notes sessions may grow.
[03:28] [03:28] Liam: (console) Here's the sim: option A cost = $X per 1M tokens baseline, option B shows ~38% token reduction for templated paths. Option C adds a small per-session memory overhead but increases throughput by ~15% because the runtime avoids re-computing KV rows.
[03:45] Jon: Those percentages look great — how do you measure template hit rate?
[03:49] Liam: We ingest prompt logs and run a clustering heuristic in Optimize. It outputs a top-k prefix list and an estimated hit rate based on historical frequency. Hit rate accuracy depends on prompt variance — more templated apps get better results.
[04:02] [04:02] Priya: One concern — our clinicians often edit the template. If they change a single word at the start, will the prefix miss and you lose savings?
[04:10] Liam: Great question. We provide fuzzy-prefix grouping; the engine supports n-gram similarity and some semantic cluster thresholds. So if edits are small, you'll still hit a prefix bucket. We'll show a brief example.
[04:22] (Liam types) [04:27] Liam: Example: base template A and variant A2 differ by 3 tokens, similarity 0.82 — we still prefetch a merged snapshot and we store a small delta patch to be applied at runtime.
[04:39] Samir: Is that delta applied server-side? Any customization needed on the client?
[04:44] Liam: Server-side. No client changes except setting routing to your private endpoint and optionally annotating known template IDs.
[04:51] [04:51] Maya: Quick segue to latency SLOs — with prefix prefetch on our 4096 model in east-us-2, we commonly see median 90–120ms and p95 < 220ms depending on batch window. With KV warmers tuned, p95 can be nudged under 180ms for mostly templated traffic.
[05:08] Dana (Security): How about auditability — we need per-request logs to be exported to our SIEM, and we need to redact PHI.
[05:16] Harper: We support log forwarding to your syslog/Splunk via private endpoints and we provide on-the-fly PII redaction hooks before logs leave the VPC. We'll include the redaction config examples.
[05:30] [05:30] Liam: Now I'm going to run a live simulation in the console. I'm toggling prefetch on for the top-10 prefixes and bumping batch size from 8 to 16 for off-peak. You'll see token delta and cost curves.
[05:45] (small lag while console sim runs) [06:10] Liam: Alright results loaded — baseline RPS under small traffic shows throughput 120 RPS, cost per 1k requests $Y. With prefetch the effective tokens per request drop by 46% on templated subset, overall cost per 1k requests drops ~22%. Batch size increase yields marginal extra savings but increases median latency by ~20ms.
[06:35] Priya: If we need p95 < 180ms during peak, what's the recommended approach?
[06:40] Liam: For peak windows keep batch window minimal (e.g., 10ms batching), use prefix prefetch for templated calls, and rely on dedicated capacity or reserved instances for consistent tail latencies. Also consider smaller model shards with higher concurrency if throughput is huge.
[06:58] [06:58] Maya: We can also set smart routing policies: route high-priority traffic to dedicated nodes while spilling best-effort to cheaper hosts. That keeps SLA traffic low-latency.
[07:08] Samir: Cost question — are the KV snapshot storage costs charged separately? How do we model snapshot GB-month?
[07:15] Liam: Snapshot storage is billed separately at a low monthly rate — in the sim I included a line for estimated snapshot storage based on top-k list size. For typical workloads it's a small fraction (<5%) of inference costs. We'll provide a breakdown by token vs snapshot vs reserved capacity.
[07:31] [07:31] Jon: Any gotchas for multi-tenant datasets? We have patients from multiple hospitals and need strict tenant isolation.
[07:38] Harper: In Private deployments we isolate KV caches per-tenant and can map snapshots to tenant-specific KMS keys. RBAC controls ensure only authorized services can access snapshots.
[07:50] [07:50] (noise, short pause)
[08:00] Liam: Moving on — concurrency and batching tradeoffs. Here's a small chart: x-axis concurrency, y-axis cost per 1k tokens. You can see diminishing returns beyond concurrency 40 for the selected GPU type.
[08:14] Priya: Our peak RPS is 350 — what concurrency do you suggest?
[08:19] Liam: For 350 RPS we recommend concurrency ~24 per worker with autoscale to add workers in burst windows. We'll size reserved capacity to handle base load and autoscale for peaks.
[08:30] [08:30] Maya: Another note: quantization recommendations — in Optimize we suggest q4_0 for many 8k models which keeps quality high but cuts GPU memory allowing higher packing. That affects batch packing efficiency.
[08:42] Samir: We have to validate quality — do you run evals on our prompts?
[08:46] Liam: Yes, we can run a quick eval harness against your sample prompt set to surface regression risk before recommending quantization. That will be part of the pilot.
[08:56] [08:56] (Priya types link in chat) Priya: Here's sample prompt set (link to S3 placeholder) — please use for eval.
[09:04] Liam: Got it — we'll pull it into the eval runner.
[09:08] [09:08] Dana: One more security question — during prefetching are snapshots ever replicated outside the region for warm pools?
[09:17] Harper: By default warm pools live in the same region but if you enable cross-region replication for failover that's an opt-in and we'll respect your KMS controls. We'll document default behavior.
[09:28] [09:28] Maya: Ok we're about 35 minutes in — quick pivot to next steps and pilot plan. Proposed: 2-week pilot (sandbox Private deployment in east-us-2), run 1 week of live traffic with prefix prefetch enabled for top-10 templates, measure p50/p95 latency and cost delta.
[09:48] Priya: Timeline-wise we aim to start pilot within 10 business days of legal/PO sign-off. We have a quarterly budget review next week but prelim OK.
[09:58] Maya: Great. We'll send a tailored cost simulation (CSV) and security package (SOC2 docs, KMS integration guide). Liam will run an eval on your sample prompts and provide quantization/pack recommendations.
[10:12] [10:12] (short overlapping chatter) Jon: Any competitor notes we should worry about? We evaluated X last year but they didn't have prefix prefetch baked in.
[10:20] Maya: Noted. We'll also include a short competitive appendix.
[10:25] [10:25] Liam: Last thing — a brief demo of failure modes: if a prefetch snapshot is stale we automatically fall back to full compute with a temporary latency bump, and we track regression metrics and can auto-disable a snapshot if quality drops.
[10:40] Samir: Good. That behavior is important to avoid silently returning stale suggestions.
[10:46] [10:46] Maya: Alright let's capture action items and wrap. Thanks everyone.
[10:52] Priya: Thanks, this was helpful.
[10:55] (call ends)
